title-group.article-title: Choice and Death: Analysis of Medical Assistance in Dying for Head and Neck Cancer in Ontario

sec.title: Objective
sec.p: There is a paucity of information on the uptake of Medical Assistance in Dying (MAiD) for patients with head and neck cancer (HNC). Our study reports the prevalence, disease characteristics, and nature of the desire for MAiD in patients with HNC who underwent the process in Ontario. The aim is to better understand this population and identify gaps in our current system of care.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This is a retrospective cross‐sectional analysis for the period June 17, 2016 to December 31, 2022. Data were received from the Office of the Chief Coroner Ontario, Canada.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Three hundred and fifty‐six persons received MAiD. The average age was 72.4 years (SD 12.22) with 260 of the patients being men (73.03%). The most common HNC primary tumor site was the oral cavity 109 (30.6%). The most reported reason was inadequate control of symptoms other than pain (79.21%) followed by inadequate pain control or concerns about it (75%). The patient's private residence (55.62%) was the most common setting. Patients were more likely to live in wealthier neighborhoods and in large urban centers. Future prediction of MAiD uptake shows a linear year‐by‐year increase.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: The use of MAiD in HNC has been steadily increasing since its legalization and is projected to continue increasing. There is a male predominance that is aligned with the incidence and prevalence of HNC nationally. Overall, MAiD is an increasingly employed choice for HNC patients receiving treatment for disease without curative intent.

abstract.p: The uptake of MAiD for head and neck cancer (HNC) has been steadily increasing since 2016, when MAiD first became available in Canada. Our study projects a substantial increase in the future use of MAiD for patients with HNC. As such, our health system needs to re‐evaluate and implement the necessary infrastructure to support the projected increase in patient demand for MAiD access.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Canada's Medical Assistance in Dying (MAiD) became legal in Canada when Bill C‐14 received Royal Assent on June 17, 2016 to establish the legal eligibility criteria and procedural safeguards for those seeking MAiD [1].

Head and neck cancers (HNCs) can be complex and, when advanced, debilitating and can significantly impact a patient's quality of life. Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is a group of malignancies involving the upper aerodigestive tract (specifically divided into the following subsites: oral cavity, pharynx, hypopharynx, larynx, nasal cavity, and salivary glands) that represent the seventh most common cancer diagnosed worldwide [2]. With the rising incidence of HNC there is the concern about the increasing burden of disease. For patients with incurable HNC the end‐of‐life phase is uniquely challenging due to the anatomical and functional location of tumors as disease in the head and neck region may result in a number of issues such as airway compromise, swallowing dysfunction, pain, disfigurement, and other symptoms that significantly reduce quality of life [3].

In Canada, according to the Fourth Annual report on MAiD, 13,241 persons accessed MAiD in 2022 with the majority (63%) of persons having a type of cancer as their main underlying medical condition [4]. In this report, HNC is grouped under the category of “other cancers” which accounts for 9% of all MAiD deaths. However, little information is provided on the details of this category.

Worldwide, only a limited number of jurisdictions have legalized MAiD, including Canada, several European nations (the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg, Switzerland, Spain, and Austria), Colombia, New Zealand, Australia, Ecuador, and select US states such as Oregon and Washington [5, 6, 7]. Most reports categorize HNC under “other malignancies,” making disease‐specific MAiD rates difficult to determine [8, 9, 10, 11, 12]. Where reported, HNC accounts for approximately 1.9% of MAiD cases in Belgium [13] and 2% in Oregon [14]. In contrast, one tertiary center in Ontario reported HNC in nearly 7% of all malignancy‐related MAiD requests [15]. Only one study has specifically examined HNC patients receiving MAiD, as study from Oregon that examined 57 patients [16]. In addition there was also a study from Eastern Ontario where 22% of nonmetastatic cancer patients requesting MAiD had HNC [17], reflecting the substantial symptom burden associated with advanced head and neck disease.

This critical literature gap limits our ability to understand the unique challenges of HNC patients at the end of life that may influence their utilization of MAiD. A recent Canadian study [18] highlights the broader issue of incomplete characterization of MAiD users even at the provincial level, noting substantial variability in reporting and limited condition‐specific details. Findings from this study underscore how little is known about the experiences of subgroups such as patients with HNC, despite their high disease burden, complex symptomatology, and significant functional decline. A clearer understanding of MAiD utilization in HNC is needed to support healthcare providers, policymakers, patients, and families by identifying unmet needs, informing service planning, and guiding improvements in end‐of‐life care delivery. Our study aimed to describe the demographic and disease characteristics of the patients with HNC who underwent MAiD in Ontario. We looked to identify the main reasons for requesting MAiD and to increase our knowledge and understanding of the current system of care.

sec.title: Study Design
sec.p: We conducted a retrospective review of all patients who received MAiD in Ontario from June 17, 2016 to December 31, 2022, who had primary mucosal SCC of the HNC as the reason for MAiD. Patients with a primary endocrine tumors, for example, thyroid or who had distant mets to H&N were excluded. Data were obtained from the Office of the Chief Coroner for Ontario (OCC). The OCC is Health Canada's designated recipient of information at the time of a MAiD death in Ontario. The data obtained from the OCC included the patient's age, sex, postal code, HNC diagnosis, nature of the physical and/or psychological suffering leading to the MAiD request, and the setting where MAiD took place.

We used descriptive statistics to summarize the data, including frequencies, percentages, means, and standard deviations. Chi‐squared test analyses were used to compare categorical data. Analysis was performed using Stata 12 (College Station, TX: StataCorp LP).

We used the Postal Code Conversion File Plus, Version 8B (PCCF+) program [19] to determine after‐tax neighborhood income quintiles and rural residence status based on individuals' postal codes. Chi‐squared goodness‐of‐fit tests were used to evaluate the distribution of MAiD cases across categories. p values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant. For the future prediction data, temporal trends in MAiD case volume were assessed by aggregating case counts per calendar year and visualized using line plots. To estimate future case volumes, a simple linear regression model was applied to annual case counts and projected values up to the year 2032.
This study was approved by the Ottawa Health Science Network Research Ethics Board (Protocol 20240137‐01H).

sec.title: Demographics
sec.p: During the study period, 356 persons with HNC received MAiD in Ontario. The average age was 72.4 years (SD 12.22) and the majority (n = 260) were men (73.03%). Since Canadian adults were first allowed to receive MAiD in 2016, there has been a steady increase in the procedure over the years. In 2017, the first full year that MAiD was available, 25 persons with HNC requested and received MAiD. By 2022, this number rose to 96, which represents an increase of almost 300% (Figure 1).

caption.p: Number of MAiD deaths in Ontario related to head and neck cancer. [Color figure can be viewed in the online issue, which is available at www.laryngoscope.com]

sec.p: The distribution of MAiD cases varied significantly by both neighborhood income quintile and geographic area (p < 0.01). A higher proportion of cases were observed in higher‐income neighborhoods, with 26.1% of cases residing in the highest income quintile compared to 18.3% in the lowest quintile. Most individuals (53.7%) lived in large urban population centers (≥ 100,000 residents), while smaller proportions resided in rural areas (18.3%), small population centers (16.3%), and medium population centers (10.4%). These findings suggest that individuals receiving MAiD due to HNC were more likely to live in wealthier neighborhoods and large urban centers.

A simple linear regression showed that if the year‐by‐year increase follows the trend shown since 2016, 211 provisions of MAiD related to HNC are expected in the year 2030 and 240 in the year 2032 (Figure 2).

caption.p: Projected number of MAiD deaths related to head and neck cancer.

sec.title: MAiD HNC Sites
sec.p: A specific site for HNC was available for 320 patients. The most common HNC site was the oral cavity (30.6%) with the tongue being the most common subsite (49.54%). The second most common site was pharynx (27.25%); of those, 64.95% had cancer located in the oropharynx. For patients diagnosed with oropharyngeal cancer, the exact subsite was unspecified in 40 cases (41.24%) and when specified, tonsils were the most common subsite with a total of 22 cases (22.68%) (Table 1).

caption.p: Site of head and neck cancer.

sec.title: Reasons for MAiD
sec.p: Most patients reported more than one reason for choosing MAiD with 95.5% reporting two or more reasons. The most common reason for MAiD was inadequate control of symptoms other than pain (79.21%). These symptoms included uncontrolled dyspnea, hemoptysis, and tolerating secretions. The second most cited reason was inadequate pain control or concerns about it (75%) and the third was the loss of ability to perform activities of daily living (ADLs) (59.27%). Men were more likely than women (p = 0.038) to report “perceived burden on family, friends, and caregivers” as a reason to request MAiD (Figure 3).

caption.p: Reason for requesting MAiD by sex. [Color figure can be viewed in the online issue, which is available at www.laryngoscope.com]

sec.title: Provision of MAiD
sec.p: The average time between the submission of the written request and the provision of MAiD was 32.4 days (0–1063 days). Most patients had MAiD at a private residence (55.62%) while smaller proportions underwent MAiD at a hospital (23.03%) or palliative care facility (15.73%) (Figure 4). MAiD setting did not differ based on the primary HNC sites.

caption.p: MAiD setting. [Color figure can be viewed in the online issue, which is available at www.laryngoscope.com]

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Until now there has been no study in the Canadian setting that looks specifically at patients who have used MAiD for primary HNC. From review of the literature of jurisdictions globally that have a similar process to MAiD only one study was found that looked specifically at HNC. This was from Oregon where 57 patients were prescribed physician‐assisted suicide (PAS) medication under the Death with Dignity Act (DWDA) between the period 1998 and 2018, and 68% ingested the medication, while 31.6% did not, despite being prescribed the medication to end their lives. Primary sites included oral cavity (33%), oropharynx (31%), larynx (23%), hypopharynx (5%), nasopharynx (5%), and salivary gland (3%). Most patients were male (69%) with a mean age of 69.4 years. The predominant concerns prompting MAiD were loss of enjoyable activities (79.5%) and loss of autonomy (74.4%). When they compared the group who died by lethal drug administration versus those who did not use the prescription, they found no significant differences between the groups aside from the patients who used the prescription tended to have lower educational attainment compared to those who did not (p = 0.015). By contrast, in our study the coroner's office is only informed of patients who received MAiD, not those who were assessed but did not chose to receive MAiD [16].
Both globally and from data for our study it is evident that there is limited information available about MAiD and HNC not only in Canada but worldwide.

On a national scale, Health Canada is the government body tasked with the collection of information for the purposes of monitoring MAiD. However, despite HNC being one of the top 10 most common cancer diagnosis worldwide [2], Health Canada collects this data under its “other cancer” category. This reveals low prioritization of data collection for an important and prevalent cancer and further limits our ability to understand MAiD use in this patient group.

The expected incidence of HNC in Canada for 2024 was 8100 cases, with 5800 (71.6%) cases occurring in men and 2300 (28.4%) in women [20]. Further, between 1993 and 2018 there were 47,700 cases of HNC in Canada, with 70.4% occurring in men and 29.6% in women [21]. Our analysis showed that 73% of HNC patients undergoing MAiD were men which appears to be aligned with the incidence and prevalence of HNC in the Canadian population.

In Ontario, 356 patients underwent MAiD for HNC between June 2016 and December 31, 2022. According to Statistics Canada the average population of Ontario was 14.2 million in 2020. In Belgium the population was 11.5 million and HNC patients accounted for ~1.9% of all MAiD cases between 2018 and 2021 [13]. The absolute number of HNC patients receiving MAiD in the country of Belgium is roughly comparable to or smaller than Ontario's provincial absolute number. For Oregon the population was 4.2 million in 2020 [22] and HNC accounted for ~2% of PAS between 1998 and 2018 [14]. The absolute number of HNC patients accessing PAS is smaller than for the province of Ontario. This highlights that Ontario sees a substantial number of HNC patients accessing MAiD, which is significant enough to merit attention, given it is only a fraction of HNC MAiD deaths in Canada.

When MAiD provisions in Canada were compared between provinces, Ontario accounted for ~30.3% of all MAiD cases followed by Quebec (36.5%) and British Columbia (18.0%). These three provinces made up nearly 85% of all MAiD cases nationally.

The increase in MAiD due to HNC over the years in the studied cohort is consistent with the pattern of increase of total MAiD deaths in Canada. The average rate of increase of MAiD in Canada was 31.1% from 2019 to 2022 [4]. In the HNC population, the average increase was 31.4% between 2017 and 2022. In Ontario specifically, the 2022 report noted a 26.8% year‐over‐year increase in MAiD provisions. Additionally, in March 2021 Bill C‐7 came into effect removing the requirement for a person's natural death to be reasonably foreseeable. Although the percentage of those receiving MAiD under the new legislation is small, it could potentially contribute to an increase in MAiD access in the coming years.

If the rate of increase of MAiD provisions follows the same trajectory observed in the first 6 years, we expect to have 240 patients access MAiD due to HNC in the year 2032. This data may exceed expectations of MAiD deaths for HNC and lead one to question whether the system is equipped to handle this increase. Health Canada initially predicted that “Canada would reach a steady state growth in total deaths attributed to MAiD from 2023 to 2033, reaching 4% of total deaths in 2033.” However, in 2022 that 4% rate was exceeded. In fact, Canada's assisted‐dying program is the fastest growing in the world [23]. Understanding this projected increase is important to evaluating and refining the multidisciplinary approach to the MAiD process and equipping the system with the necessary resources for this increase. Health Canada would be the ideal repository national source for streamlining HNC information as well as assessing this potential increase and implementing strategies to mitigate this increase.

Our analysis found that individuals with HNC receiving MAiD were more likely to live in wealthier neighborhoods and in large urban centers. In contrast, the incidence of HNC has been associated with lower SES [2, 24, 25]. In addition Tran et al. [26] examined MAiD requests at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) in Ontario and found that more MAiD requests came from lower‐SES areas −58.1%, while 41.9% came from higher‐SES areas. By contrast, Redelmeier et al. [27], using a case–control study of palliative‐care patients in Ontario, found that low‐SES patients were less likely to receive MAiD. The association of a higher SES with the use of MAiD in HNC in our study is unclear. It has been shown that patients with a lower SES may feel less empowered and have lower health literacy, potentially leading to reduced self‐advocacy and diminished trust in the health care system [28, 29]. Health literacy along with education, income, financial stability, geography, insurance and access can affect patient–clinician interactions, health outcomes, and a patient's ability to obtain, process, understand, and use health information [30]. Our findings may therefore highlight SES as a potential modifying factor to the social component of access and undergoing the MAiD process. However, given the conflicting reports across studies, we cannot make any definitive conclusions. More targeted studies in this area are needed to better understand the relationship between SES and MAiD use in HNC.

Our study found that men were twice more likely than women to cite a perceived burden on family, friends, and caregivers as a reason to request MAiD. According to McPherson et al., feeling like a burden is a major concern for many people near the end of life which can lead to the feeling of creating hardships for loved ones [31]. A systematic review found that for 19%–65% of terminally ill patients, feeling like a burden is a significant problem. This feeling can impact choices about type and location of care as well as choices to speed up death [32]. There is limited data about the perception of caregiver burden by HNC patients and given the findings of this study, it is an area for further research. Recommendations that can be considered for patients with HNC include the potential added importance of family meetings for men and their family or caregivers. This could create open discussions about the perceived burden for caregivers and how best this can be mitigated.

The most common reasons to request MAiD cited by HNC patients differed from the reasons given by all patients having MAiD in Canada. Between 2019 and 2022, the most frequent reason for MAiD was the inability to engage in meaningful life activities followed by the loss of ability to perform ADLs. Our data show that the most common reasons cited by HNC patients for requesting MAiD is inadequate control of symptoms other than pain (79.21%) followed by inadequate pain control or concern about it. HNC presents with particularly distressing symptoms that, when inadequately controlled, significantly impact a patient's health‐related quality of life. These include dysphagia, dyspnea/shortness of breath, control of secretions, hemoptysis with many of these patients requiring high level medical interventions such as feeding tubes and tracheostomy. A study assessing the correlation between symptom burden and perceived distress in advanced HNC showed that outpatient palliative care consultations provided for significant improvement in symptom and distress score [33]. This suggests that there needs to be an increased understanding of the complex nature of the symptom burden which should prompt us to pay more attention to integrated care with particular focus on advance care planning and early palliative intervention as well as the upskilling of healthcare professionals in different care settings. Current Canadian MAiD legislation does not mandate a legal requirement to refer every MAiD requester to palliative care. Specifically, where death is reasonably foreseeable, patients must be informed of palliative care as a management option. However, where natural death is not reasonably foreseeable, the person must be informed of available means to relieve suffering, including palliative care, and be offered consultations with relevant professionals.

Although to our knowledge this study is the first to present robust data on the use of MAiD by patients with HNC in Canada, our study does have some limitations. This study is a retrospective cross‐sectional study, and its retrospective nature lends it to all possible biases associated with this methodology. Further, while we did get sociodemographic data captured by the coroner's office for patients who underwent MAiD, this information was limited, and we were unable to fully capture the essence of the socioeconomic status of the patients. We were also unable to ascertain the timing of the MAiD request to the disease stage and the provision of MAiD. With these shortcomings, it is unclear as to the equity of access to the procedure. Since January 1, 2023, Health Canada expanded its data collection for the monitoring of MAiD to include information on gender, race, Indigenous identity, and disability, which will be collected only if the person consents to providing this information. This will create much needed data moving forward for further analysis and informing inequities to access and usership of MAiD.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: We obtained valuable insights into the decision‐making processes surrounding end‐of‐life care for individuals with HNC. We now know that MAiD is an option for patients with HNC, especially for those with disease that is without cure. Healthcare providers need to be equipped with the knowledge and be comfortable to have informed discussions with a person on the lawful provision of the procedure. The uptake of MAiD has been steadily increasing since it first became available, which could signify both greater awareness and accessibility to the process. There is a projected increase in future use for HNC, and as such the health system needs to re‐evaluate and implement the necessary infrastructure to sustain this increase. As our study is limited to Ontario, further research on a national scale is needed. This will require improved data collection by Health Canada to be best able to evaluate MAiD access and use in patients with HNC.
